scenes.text: You leave a banana on the kitchen counter and forget about it for a few days. It goes brown. Then black. It starts to smell.
And then, one morning, there are tiny flies circling it. A few days ago, there wasn't a single fly in the kitchen. So where did they come from?
Did you just witness life appearing from nothing?
They're fruit flies. And they're drawn to fermenting fruit, and to the yeast growing on it. The smell can pull them in from outside.
Some slip in through a gap in a window. Some ride in as eggs on other fruit you brought home.
And once a few are in, they breed. In warm conditions, it takes about ten days from egg to flying adult. And one female can lay around five hundred eggs.
So nothing appeared out of nowhere. Every one of those flies hatched from an egg laid by another fly.
That sounds obvious. But it took people more than two thousand years to work it out. And the answer left behind a problem we still haven't solved.
Because if life only ever comes from life... where did the first life come from?
For most of history, the answer to the kitchen mystery was much simpler. Life could just start on its own.
More than two thousand years ago, Aristotle wrote that eels grew out of mud, and that some insects formed from dew falling on leaves.
The idea is called spontaneous generation, and it lasted for centuries.
In the 1600s, the Flemish chemist Jan Baptist van Helmont even wrote down a recipe for mice.
Put some dirty underwear in a jar of wheat. Wait twenty-one days. And mice will appear.
And to be fair, it looks convincing. Leave grain in a barn, and mice eventually appear. But the barn already had mice.
In 1668, an Italian physician called Francesco Redi decided to stop arguing and start watching.
He put pieces of meat into jars. Some he left open. Some he sealed shut. The open jars filled with maggots. The sealed ones didn't.
But there was an obvious objection. Sealing the jar also cut off the air. Maybe life needed fresh air to start.
So Redi covered some jars with fine gauze instead. Air could get in. Flies couldn't.
No maggots in the meat. But maggots on top of the gauze, dropped there by flies that couldn't get in.
The meat wasn't making life. The flies were.
That should have settled it. But a few years later, microscopes revealed a whole world of tiny living things.
And they seemed to turn up in any broth left out, with no eggs anyone could see. So maybe spontaneous generation still worked... just smaller.
Almost two hundred years after Redi, in 1859, Louis Pasteur took on the question in Paris.
He filled glass flasks with broth, heated their necks and bent them into a long curve, like the neck of a swan.
Then he boiled the broth to kill anything already in it. Air could still get in through the open end.
But the dust and microbes drifting in with it settled in the bend of the neck, and never reached the broth.
The broth stayed clear. For months. For years.
Then he broke the neck off a flask, so the dust could fall straight in. Within a day or two, it was cloudy.
In 1864, Pasteur told an audience at the Sorbonne that spontaneous generation would never recover from this blow.
Life comes from life. And that is exactly what's happening on your kitchen counter.
But look at what that did to the bigger question.
Around the same time, Charles Darwin argued that every living thing descends from earlier living things.
Put Pasteur and Darwin together, and you get a chain. Life from life, back and back, for billions of years... and it can't go on forever.
Earth formed about four and a half billion years ago. At first it was far too hot for anything to survive.
The oldest widely accepted traces of life are about three and a half billion years old. Layered rocks in Western Australia, built up by mats of microbes.
So at some point, on a planet with no life at all, something that wasn't alive became something that was.
Scientists call that step abiogenesis. And it seems to clash with everything Pasteur proved.
But Pasteur never showed that life can't come from chemistry. He showed it doesn't happen in a swan-neck flask, even after years.
The early Earth had hundreds of millions of years, and whole oceans to work with. And it had one more advantage.
Darwin spotted it in a letter in 1871. Today, he wrote, any chemistry on its way to life would be devoured instantly.
Your banana never stood a chance. Yeast got to it first. Then the flies came for the yeast.
Before the first life, there was nothing to get there first.
In that same letter, Darwin began with a warning: oh, what a big if. Then he imagined a warm little pond, with ammonia and salts, light, heat and electricity.
In 1952, a student called Stanley Miller, working with Harold Urey, tried to fill in that if.
He sealed water, methane, ammonia and hydrogen in glass, heated it, and fired sparks through it to stand in for lightning.
After a week, the water had turned a murky red. And in it were amino acids, the building blocks of proteins.
In 2008, researchers re-tested vials from a steamier version of his experiment, and found more than twenty amino acids.
Miller's gases were probably not quite what the early atmosphere held. But other mixtures make building blocks too. And so does space.
In 1969, a meteorite fell near Murchison, in Australia. Inside it were more than seventy kinds of amino acids.
So the ingredients aren't the hard part. Chemistry makes them on its own, on Earth and off it.
The hard part is the next step. A heap of building blocks isn't alive, the same way a bag of letters isn't a book.
Life has to carry instructions. And it has to copy them.
In your cells, that's a team effort. DNA stores the instructions. Proteins do the work, including copying the DNA.
But proteins are built from DNA's instructions. And DNA is copied by proteins. So which came first?
In 1982, Thomas Cech found a molecule that broke the loop. A piece of RNA, DNA's chemical cousin, that could cut and join itself with no protein involved.
RNA can carry instructions, like DNA. And some RNA can do work, like a protein. One molecule, both jobs.
That's the idea behind what's called the RNA world. Early life may have run on RNA, before DNA and proteins took over.
And there's a clue inside every one of your cells. Every protein in your body was put together by a machine whose working heart is RNA.
In 2026, researchers reported a tiny RNA called QT45. From ready-made pieces, it can build a copy of itself. But no RNA has yet been shown to keep copying itself, round after round.
And nobody knows where it happened. A warm pond, drying out and filling up again? Or hot vents on the dark ocean floor?
Each idea has serious scientists behind it. None of them has the whole answer.
But maybe the question itself is set up the wrong way.
Where did the first life come from? That assumes there was a first. One moment, one thing, that wasn't alive, and then was.
So what counts as alive? One working definition, developed by NASA scientists, describes life as a self-sustaining chemical system capable of Darwinian evolution.
Picture a molecule that makes rough copies of itself. Some copies come out a little different.
Some of them copy faster than others. And if those differences are inherited, the faster copies become more common.
Is that alive? It's not a cell. It doesn't eat or breathe. But it's already evolving.
Now add a membrane around it. Then a way to grab energy. Then a better copier. At which step did it come alive?
It's a bit like asking who spoke the first word of French. Nobody did. Spoken Latin just slowly drifted, until one day it was French.
Life may be the same. Not a spark.
A slope.
Chemistry that got a little more like life, again and again, until there was no going back.
And here's the strangest part. The fly, the banana, the yeast and you all use essentially the same genetic code.
That points to a common ancestor. But a common ancestor isn't necessarily the first life.
It doesn't tell us whether life began only once, or whether other beginnings simply left no survivors. The best way to find out may be to find life that started somewhere else.
So next time fruit flies turn up around a forgotten banana, they're not life appearing from nothing.
They're the newest link in a chain that hasn't broken once in about three and a half billion years.
And at the far end of that chain, there's no first fly. Maybe no first anything. Just chemistry, slowly getting better at copying itself.
So here's a question for you. If a lab one day made something that copies itself and evolves, starting from nothing but simple chemicals, would you call it alive? Let me know in the comments.
